features.name: Card Initialization
features.description:
## Card Initialization (F_INIT)

**Purpose:** Card Initialization encompasses the complete sequence required to detect, identify, and configure an SDIO card for operation after power-up or reset. This includes sending CMD5 (IO_SEND_OP_COND) to query card capabilities, negotiating operating voltage, obtaining the Relative Card Address (RCA), and transitioning the card from idle state to ready for data transfer.

**Behavior:** The host controller executes the initialization sequence by first issuing CMD5 with zero argument to detect SDIO presence and read supported voltage ranges (R4 response), then re-issuing CMD5 with the selected operating voltage to complete initialization. For combo cards containing both I/O and memory functions, special handling ensures both portions are properly initialized while managing RCA assignment and CRC settings appropriately.

features.name: Non-I/O Aware Initialization
features.description:
## F_INIT_NON_IO (Non-I/O Aware Initialization)

**Purpose:** This feature implements the initialization sequence used when an SDIO card is inserted into a standard SD memory host that is not aware of SDIO I/O functionality. The host follows the standard SD memory card initialization flow without issuing CMD5 (IO_SEND_OP_COND), treating the card purely as a memory device.

**Behavior:** When a non-I/O aware host initializes an SDIO combo card, only the memory portion of the card becomes accessible while the I/O functions remain dormant. For SDIO-only cards (no memory), the card will fail initialization since the host cannot recognize or communicate with the I/O portion, as specified in section 3.1.1 of the SDIO specification.

features.name: I/O Aware Initialization
features.description:
## I/O Aware Initialization (F_INIT_IO_AWARE)

**Purpose:** Implements the SDIO-specific initialization sequence where the host actively probes for I/O functionality using CMD5 (IO_SEND_OP_COND) before falling back to standard SD memory card initialization.

**Behavior:** An I/O aware host sends CMD5 first during card detection to identify SDIO or combo cards, processes the R4 response to determine I/O capabilities and voltage requirements, and properly initializes the card's I/O functions. This contrasts with non-I/O aware hosts that skip CMD5 and only recognize memory card functionality, as detailed in section 3.1.2 of the SDIO specification.

features.name: IO_SEND_OP_COND (CMD5)
features.description:
## IO_SEND_OP_COND (CMD5) - Feature Description

**IO_SEND_OP_COND (CMD5)** is the primary initialization command used by I/O-aware hosts to detect and initialize SDIO cards. When sent, the host provides its supported voltage range in the argument, and the card responds with an R4 response containing the card's operating conditions, number of I/O functions, memory present bit, and card ready status.

This command serves dual purposes: with a zero argument, it queries the card's capabilities without initiating voltage negotiation; with a valid voltage argument, it begins the initialization process where the card compares supported voltages and sets its ready bit when initialization completes. The host must poll CMD5 until the card indicates ready (C bit set in R4) before proceeding with further initialization steps like obtaining the RCA via CMD3.

features.name: R4 Response
features.description:
## F_R4_RESPONSE (R4 Response)

**Purpose:** The R4 Response is the specific response format returned by SDIO cards in reply to the IO_SEND_OP_COND command (CMD5) during the initialization sequence.

**Behavior:** The R4 response contains critical information for SDIO card initialization, including the card's ready status bit (C bit), number of I/O functions supported, memory present flag (for combo cards), and the card's supported operating condition register (OCR) voltage range. The host uses this response to determine if the card is ready for operation and to negotiate compatible voltage levels before proceeding with further initialization steps like assigning a relative card address (RCA).

features.name: Combo Card Initialization
features.description:
## Combo Card Initialization (F_COMBO_INIT)

**Purpose:** This feature handles the specialized initialization sequence required for SDIO Combo Cards, which contain both I/O functions and memory storage on a single card, requiring coordinated initialization of both subsystems.

**Behavior:** The initialization process must properly detect and configure both the I/O and memory portions of a combo card, handling scenarios such as re-initializing both subsystems (Section 3.4.1), operating the card in SDIO-only or SD Memory-only mode after combo initialization (Section 3.4.2), and managing RCA (Relative Card Address) assignment recommendations after reset (Section 3.4.4). The host must issue appropriate commands in the correct sequence to ensure both card functions are properly enumerated and accessible.

features.name: Bus Transfer Modes
features.description:
## Bus Transfer Modes (F_BUS_MODES)

Bus Transfer Modes defines the supported data transfer configurations between the SDIO host controller and connected cards, including **SPI mode**, **1-bit SD mode**, and **4-bit SD mode**. The controller must detect card capabilities and configure the appropriate bus width, with 1-bit mode being mandatory for all cards while 4-bit mode is required for high-speed cards and optional for low-speed devices. This feature governs the fundamental data path width negotiation and signal routing that directly impacts achievable throughput and compatibility across different SDIO card types.

features.name: SPI Mode
features.description:
## F_SPI_MODE (SPI Mode)

SPI Mode is a mandatory card-supported bus interface that provides a simplified 4-wire serial communication protocol (CS, CLK, DI, DO) as an alternative to the native SD bus interface. This mode offers universal compatibility with microcontrollers and embedded systems that have standard SPI peripherals but lack dedicated SD host controllers.

As specified in section 2.2.1, SPI mode trades off performance for simplicity—it operates at lower speeds than native SD modes but requires minimal hardware support and uses a straightforward command/response protocol with optional CRC checking (which can be enabled for combo cards per section 3.4.5).

features.name: 1-bit SD Mode
features.description:
Based on the SDIO specification context, here is the description for this feature:

## F_SD_1BIT: 1-bit SD Mode

**Purpose:** Implements the mandatory 1-bit SD data transfer mode where data is transferred serially over a single DAT0 line, providing basic SD protocol communication with minimal pin requirements.

**Behavior:** In 1-bit SD mode, the host uses the CMD line for commands/responses and only the DAT0 line for data transfers, operating with the standard SD clock. This mode is mandatory for all SDIO cards and serves as the default transfer mode after card initialization before optionally switching to 4-bit mode. It provides compatibility with simpler host implementations and is the fallback mode when wider bus widths are not supported or during initial card enumeration.

features.name: 4-bit SD Mode
features.description:
## F_SD_4BIT: 4-bit SD Mode

**Purpose:** Enables parallel data transfer using 4 data lines (DAT0-DAT3) simultaneously, quadrupling the effective data throughput compared to 1-bit mode while maintaining the same clock frequency.

**Behavior:** When enabled via the Bus Width field in CCCR (Card Common Control Registers), the host controller drives and samples all four DAT lines during data transfers. This mode is mandatory for High-Speed SDIO cards but optional for Low-Speed cards, as specified in section 2.2.3. The host must verify card capability through CMD52/CMD53 before switching from the default 1-bit mode.

features.name: I/O Read/Write Commands
features.description:
## F_IO_COMMANDS: I/O Read/Write Commands

**Purpose:** This feature implements the core SDIO data transfer commands (CMD52 and CMD53) that enable the host controller to read from and write to I/O function registers within an SDIO card. CMD52 provides single-byte register access, while CMD53 supports multi-byte and block data transfers with optional auto-increment addressing.

**Behavior:** The host controller must properly format and issue these I/O commands with the correct function number, register address, and read/write flags, then handle the R5 response containing status and data. For CMD53 block transfers, the controller coordinates with the block size configured in the card's Function Basic Registers (FBR) and manages the data transfer across the DAT lines according to the selected bus width mode.

features.name: IO_RW_DIRECT (CMD52)
features.description:
## IO_RW_DIRECT (CMD52) - Feature Description

**CMD52 (IO_RW_DIRECT)** is the fundamental SDIO command for performing single-byte read and write operations to any register within an SDIO card's function address space. This command provides direct, non-block-based access to the card's Common I/O Area (CIA) and function-specific registers, making it essential for configuration, status polling, and control operations.

As a P0 priority feature, CMD52 is critical for basic SDIO functionality including reading the Card Common Control Registers (CCCR), enabling/disabling I/O functions, and performing low-overhead register accesses where block transfers (CMD53) would be inefficient. The command uses the R5 response format and can optionally read back the register value after a write operation (Read-After-Write mode).

features.name: IO_RW_EXTENDED (CMD53)
features.description:
## IO_RW_EXTENDED (CMD53) - Feature Description

**CMD53 (IO_RW_EXTENDED)** is the primary data transfer command for SDIO operations, enabling multi-byte or multi-block read/write access to SDIO function registers. Unlike CMD52 which transfers only a single byte, CMD53 supports bulk data transfers with configurable block sizes and can operate in either byte mode (1-512 bytes) or block mode (1 or more blocks), making it essential for high-throughput I/O operations like WiFi or Bluetooth data streaming.

The command supports both fixed address mode (for FIFO-style access to a single register) and incrementing address mode (for accessing sequential register addresses), with the transfer direction, function number, block/byte count, and starting address all encoded in the command argument. As a P0 priority feature, it forms the foundation of all meaningful SDIO data communication beyond simple configuration register access.

features.name: CMD53 Block Mode
features.description:
## F_CMD53_BLOCK: CMD53 Block Mode

**Purpose:** CMD53 Block Mode enables multi-block data transfers where data is transferred in fixed-size blocks rather than arbitrary byte counts. This mode is essential for high-throughput SDIO operations, allowing efficient transfer of large data amounts by specifying a block count (1-511 blocks) with each block sized according to the function's configured block size.

**Behavior:** When the Block Mode bit is set in CMD53, the count field specifies the number of blocks to transfer rather than bytes. The host controller manages block boundaries, CRC checking per block, and can leverage features like infinite block transfer (count=0) for streaming applications. This mode typically achieves better performance than byte mode for transfers larger than one block size due to reduced command overhead and optimized DMA operations.

features.name: CMD53 Byte Mode
features.description:
## F_CMD53_BYTE: CMD53 Byte Mode

CMD53 Byte Mode enables data transfers of 1 to 512 bytes in a single operation without requiring block-aligned transfers, specified by setting the Block Mode bit to 0 in the CMD53 command argument. This mode is optimal for small, variable-length I/O operations typical in SDIO function register access, where the byte count field directly specifies the exact number of bytes to transfer (with a count of 0 indicating 512 bytes). As a P0 priority feature under CMD53, byte mode provides essential flexibility for efficient communication with SDIO devices when full block transfers would be wasteful or inappropriate.

features.name: R5 Response
features.description:
## F_R5_RESPONSE Feature Description

The R5 Response is the standard 48-bit response format used exclusively by SDIO cards in reply to the CMD52 (IO_RW_DIRECT) and CMD53 (IO_RW_EXTENDED) commands. This response contains critical status information including the current state of the I/O functions, error flags (CRC error, illegal command, general error), and for read operations, the 8-bit data read from the specified register address.

The R5 response format includes fields for COM_CRC_ERROR, ILLEGAL_COMMAND, IO_CURRENT_STATE (indicating whether the card is disabled, in command state, or transfer state), ERROR, FUNCTION_NUMBER, and OUT_OF_RANGE flags, enabling the host controller to verify command execution success and handle SDIO-specific error conditions appropriately.

features.name: SD Memory Compatibility
features.description:
## SD Memory Compatibility (F_SD_COMPAT)

This feature ensures the SD Host Controller maintains backward compatibility with standard SD Memory card protocols while supporting SDIO functionality. It encompasses support for SD Memory commands (as defined in section 4.2.1), proper handling of combo cards that contain both I/O and memory functions, and adherence to shared timing and signaling requirements between SD Memory and SDIO specifications.

The controller must correctly distinguish between memory-only cards, I/O-only cards, and combo cards during initialization, applying appropriate command sequences and bus configurations for each card type while maintaining interoperability with the established SD Memory ecosystem.

features.name: Supported/Unsupported Commands
features.description:
## F_CMD_SUPPORT: Supported/Unsupported Commands

This feature defines the specific set of SD/SDIO commands that the host controller must support versus those that are explicitly unsupported or handled differently for SDIO cards compared to standard SD memory cards. According to sections 4.1 and 4.2, SDIO cards support a subset of SD memory commands while introducing SDIO-specific commands (like CMD5, CMD52, CMD53), and certain memory-only commands (such as block erase or write protection commands) are explicitly unsupported on SDIO-only cards.

The host controller must correctly identify card type during initialization and restrict command issuance accordingly, ensuring that unsupported commands are not sent to SDIO cards and that SDIO-specific commands are properly formatted and processed with their unique response types.

features.name: Modified R6 Response
features.description:
Based on the specification context, particularly section 4.3 "Modified R6 Response" under "Differences with SD Memory Specification":

## Modified R6 Response (F_R6_RESPONSE)

The Modified R6 Response feature handles SDIO-specific modifications to the standard SD R6 response format used during card identification. In standard SD memory cards, R6 is returned after CMD3 (SET_RELATIVE_ADDR) and contains the new RCA and card status bits. For SDIO cards, certain status bits in the R6 response are redefined to report I/O-specific error conditions (such as COM_CRC_ERROR, ILLEGAL_COMMAND, and ERROR bits mapped to SDIO function errors) rather than memory-specific status. The host controller must correctly interpret these modified status fields to properly detect SDIO card errors during the RCA assignment phase of initialization.

features.name: Reset for SDIO
features.description:
## F_SDIO_RESET (Reset for SDIO)

**Purpose:** Implements the SDIO-specific reset mechanism that differs from standard SD memory card reset procedures, ensuring proper initialization and recovery of SDIO card functions.

**Behavior:** SDIO cards require a modified reset sequence compared to SD memory cards, as documented in section 4.4. This feature handles the reset of I/O functions within SDIO and combo cards, which may involve writing to the I/O Abort register (CCCR) or issuing CMD52 to reset specific functions, rather than relying solely on CMD0. For combo cards, special considerations apply regarding whether to reset both I/O and memory portions or selectively reset individual components while maintaining the card's relative card address (RCA) assignment.

features.name: Bus Width Control
features.description:
## Bus Width Control (F_BUS_WIDTH)

**Purpose:** Controls the data bus width configuration between the host controller and SD/SDIO cards, enabling switching between 1-bit and 4-bit data transfer modes to optimize throughput while maintaining backward compatibility.

**Behavior:** The host controller negotiates bus width capability with the card during initialization, then configures the appropriate mode by writing to both the card's Bus Width register (via CMD52 to CCCR) and the host's Bus Width field in the Host Control register. 4-bit mode is mandatory for High-Speed cards but optional for Low-Speed SDIO cards, with 1-bit mode serving as the default fallback for maximum compatibility.

features.name: Data Transfer Abort
features.description:
## Data Transfer Abort (F_DATA_ABORT)

Based on spec section **4.9 Data Transfer Abort** (with subsections 4.9.1 Read Abort and 4.9.2 Write Abort), this feature provides the mechanism to prematurely terminate an ongoing data transfer operation on the SDIO bus. It enables the host controller to cleanly abort both read and write operations when errors occur, timeouts are detected, or when the transfer is no longer needed, ensuring the bus returns to a known idle state. As a P0 compatibility feature, proper abort handling is essential for error recovery and maintaining protocol compliance with the SD specification's defined abort sequences.

features.name: Common I/O Area
features.description:
## Common I/O Area (F_CIA)

The Common I/O Area (CIA) is a mandatory register space located in Function 0 of an SDIO card that contains essential control and status registers shared across all I/O functions, including the Card Common Control Registers (CCCR) and Function Basic Registers (FBR). This area provides the host controller with standardized access to card capabilities, configuration settings, interrupt status, bus interface controls, and power management features that govern overall SDIO card operation. The CIA is accessed through CMD52 (single byte) and CMD53 (multi-byte) direct I/O commands and must be present on all SDIO-compliant cards to enable proper enumeration, configuration, and runtime management.

features.name: CCCR Registers
features.description:
Based on the specification context and standard SDIO architecture, here is the description for this feature:

## CCCR Registers (F_CCCR)

The Card Common Control Registers (CCCR) are a mandatory set of registers located in Function 0 (CIA) that provide common control and status information for the entire SDIO card. These registers enable the host to query card capabilities (SDIO version, supported bus widths, speed modes), control card-wide settings (bus interface control, power management, interrupt enables), and monitor status across all I/O functions.

The CCCR includes critical registers such as the CCCR/SDIO Revision register, SD Specification Revision, I/O Enable/Ready registers, Interrupt Enable/Pending registers, Bus Interface Control, Card Capability, and Power Control registers, forming the foundation for host-card communication and configuration.

features.name: FBR Registers
features.description:
## FBR Registers (F_FBR)

**Function Basic Registers (FBR)** are per-function register blocks located in the Card Information Area (CIA) of an SDIO card, with each of the 7 possible I/O functions having its own dedicated FBR at addresses 0xn00-0xnFF (where n is the function number 1-7). These registers contain function-specific information including the Standard SDIO Function Interface Code, Extended Standard Function Interface Code, power selection bits, and pointers to the function's Card Information Structure (CIS).

The FBR provides the host with essential metadata about each function's capabilities and requirements, enabling proper driver binding and power management for multi-function SDIO devices such as combo WiFi/Bluetooth cards.

features.name: Card Information Structure
features.description:
## Card Information Structure (F_CIS)

The Card Information Structure (CIS) is a standardized data structure stored in the SDIO card's Common I/O Area (CIA) that contains essential metadata about the card and its functions, including manufacturer identification, product information, and function-specific configuration data. The CIS uses a tuple-based format (similar to PCMCIA) where each tuple contains a type code, length, and data payload describing card capabilities, power requirements, and operational parameters. The host controller reads the CIS during initialization to determine card characteristics and properly configure the interface for optimal operation with the specific SDIO device.

features.name: Multiple Function Support
features.description:
## Multiple Function Support (F_MULTI_FUNC)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the SDIO card to support multiple independent I/O functions (up to 7 functions plus function 0 for common control), each with its own dedicated register space, interrupts, and operational capabilities within the Card Information Architecture (CIA).

**Behavior:** The host controller manages multiple functions through the Common I/O Area (CIA) registers, where each function can be individually enabled, suspended, or selected via the I/O Enable (IOEx) and Function Select bits in CCCR. Each function operates independently with its own Function Basic Registers (FBR) at dedicated address offsets, allowing simultaneous operation of different I/O peripherals (such as WiFi, Bluetooth, GPS) on a single SDIO card while sharing the common bus interface.

features.name: Block Size Setting
features.description:
## Block Size Setting (F_BLOCK_SIZE)

Based on the SDIO specification context, this feature controls the configuration of data transfer block sizes through the Card Information Area (CIA) registers. The Block Size Setting allows the host to program the number of bytes per block for I/O data transfers, with SDIO supporting flexible block sizes (typically 1-2048 bytes) that can be configured per function via the FBR (Function Basic Registers). This is a critical P0 feature because proper block size configuration directly impacts data transfer efficiency and must match between host and card for successful multi-block read/write operations as described in section 4.8 (Data Transfer Block Sizes).

features.name: Bus State Machine
features.description:
Based on the feature name, ID, and context, here is a technical description:

## Bus State Machine (F_BUS_STATE)

The Bus State Machine manages the operational states of the SDIO bus interface, tracking transitions between idle, command, data transfer, and busy states as defined by the SD/SDIO protocol. This register-based state tracking is essential for proper command/response sequencing and ensures the host controller correctly handles bus timing requirements during card initialization, data transfers, and abort operations.

As a child of the Card Interface Architecture (F_CIA), this feature provides the foundational state management that coordinates between command issuance, response reception, and data line activity, enabling the host to properly sequence operations and detect protocol violations or timeout conditions.

features.name: Code Storage Area
features.description:
# Code Storage Area (CSA) - Feature Description

The Code Storage Area (CSA) is an optional SDIO feature that provides a dedicated memory region within an SDIO card where function-specific driver code or firmware can be stored and retrieved by the host. This allows SDIO cards to carry their own driver software, enabling automatic driver loading without requiring the host to have pre-installed drivers for the specific card.

The CSA is accessed through special registers in the SDIO function's Card Information Structure (CIS) and Common I/O Area (CIA), allowing the host to read executable code or configuration data that the card manufacturer has embedded for plug-and-play functionality.

features.name: SDIO Interrupt System
features.description:
## SDIO Interrupt System (F_INTERRUPT)

The SDIO Interrupt System enables asynchronous event notification from SDIO cards to the host controller, allowing cards to signal data availability or status changes without requiring continuous polling. This mechanism uses the DAT[1] line in 4-bit mode (or DAT[0] in 1-bit mode) as an interrupt signaling path, where the card pulls the line low to assert an interrupt condition.

The host controller must detect this interrupt assertion, generate an appropriate host interrupt to the system processor, and support the interrupt handling flow including reading the card's interrupt pending registers via CMD52 to identify and service the specific function requesting attention.

features.name: Interrupt Timing
features.description:
## Interrupt Timing (F_INT_TIMING)

**Purpose:** Defines the precise timing requirements and constraints for SDIO interrupt signal generation, detection, and response to ensure reliable interrupt-driven communication between the host controller and SDIO devices.

**Behavior:** This feature specifies the timing parameters for interrupt assertion and de-assertion on the DAT[1] line (in SD mode), including minimum pulse widths, setup/hold times relative to clock edges, and maximum latency requirements for host interrupt detection. The timing specifications ensure that interrupts are not missed during high-speed data transfers and that the host can properly sample and acknowledge card-generated interrupts within defined time windows, which is critical for real-time SDIO applications like wireless networking.

features.name: 4-bit Mode Interrupts
features.description:
## 4-bit Mode Interrupts (F_INT_4BIT)

This feature enables interrupt signaling from SDIO cards when operating in 4-bit SD data transfer mode, where the DAT[1] line serves a dual purpose as both a data line and an interrupt signal line. In 4-bit mode, the card can assert an interrupt by driving DAT[1] low during idle periods between data transfers, allowing the host controller to detect card events without polling. This is a critical P0 feature as it provides the primary interrupt mechanism for high-speed SDIO operations, requiring careful arbitration between interrupt detection and normal 4-bit data transfers on the shared DAT[1] signal.

features.name: SPI/1-bit Mode Interrupts
features.description:
## SPI/1-bit Mode Interrupts (F_INT_SPI_1BIT)

This feature handles interrupt signaling mechanisms specific to SPI mode and 1-bit SD data transfer mode, which are the two mandatory card support modes defined in the SDIO specification. In SPI mode, interrupts are typically signaled through the Data Out line, while in 1-bit mode, the DAT[1] line serves as the dedicated interrupt line (SDIO_INT) since only DAT[0] is used for data transfer.

As a P0 priority interrupt feature, this provides the fundamental interrupt detection and handling capability required for basic SDIO card communication before wider bus modes (4-bit) are negotiated or when operating with legacy/low-speed cards that only support these simpler transfer modes.

features.name: Asynchronous Interrupt
features.description:
## Asynchronous Interrupt (F_ASYNC_INT)

**Purpose:** Asynchronous Interrupt enables an SDIO card to signal the host controller that it requires attention even when the SD bus clock is stopped or in a low-power state, allowing for efficient power management while maintaining responsiveness.

**Behavior:** When enabled, the SDIO card can assert an interrupt on the DAT[1] line asynchronously without requiring the host to continuously poll or maintain an active clock signal. This is particularly important for SDIO devices like WiFi or Bluetooth cards that need to wake the system upon receiving external events (such as incoming network packets) while the host is in a suspended or power-saving mode. The host controller must be configured to detect this out-of-band interrupt signaling and respond appropriately by resuming clock operation and servicing the card's interrupt request.

features.name: Suspend/Resume Operation
features.description:
## Suspend/Resume Operation (F_SUSPEND_RESUME)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the host controller to temporarily suspend an ongoing data transfer operation on one SDIO function to service a higher-priority request from another function, then resume the original transfer without data loss.

**Behavior:** When a suspend command is issued, the controller saves the current transfer state (including block count and address pointers) and halts the active operation. The host can then initiate a different command sequence. Upon issuing a resume command, the controller restores the saved context and continues the original transfer from where it was interrupted. This mechanism is essential for multi-function SDIO cards where time-critical functions (such as Bluetooth or WiFi) may need immediate attention while a lower-priority bulk transfer is in progress.

**Technical Context:** Suspend/Resume is particularly relevant for SDIO combo cards and multi-function devices, allowing efficient sharing of the single SD bus interface between functions with different latency requirements, as referenced in the SDIO specification's data transfer and abort handling sections.

features.name: Read Wait / Pause Read
features.description:
## Read Wait / Pause Read (F_READ_WAIT)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the host controller to temporarily pause an ongoing multi-block read operation from an SDIO card by asserting a signal on the DAT[2] line, allowing the host to process received data before continuing the transfer.

**Behavior:** When Read Wait is activated during a data transfer, the SDIO card suspends sending data blocks and holds the bus in a wait state. This mechanism is essential for SDIO operations where the host may need to service interrupts, handle other functions on a combo card, or manage buffer constraints without aborting the entire read operation. The transfer resumes when the host releases the read wait condition, making it particularly useful for streaming data scenarios where flow control is required.

features.name: Pause by Stopping SDCLK
features.description:
## F_RW_STOP_CLK: Pause by Stopping SDCLK

**Purpose:** This feature implements the Read Wait mechanism by stopping the SDCLK (SD Clock) signal during multi-block read operations, allowing the host to pause data transfer from an SDIO card while it processes received data.

**Behavior:** When the host needs to pause a read operation, it stops toggling the SDCLK line, which halts the card's data transmission since the card cannot clock out data without a clock signal. This is one of two methods for implementing Read Wait (the other being DAT[2] line signaling), and is typically used when the card supports this simpler clock-stopping approach rather than the DAT[2] protocol.

**Context:** As a child of F_READ_WAIT with P1 priority, this represents a fundamental implementation method for the read wait capability, essential for hosts that need to manage data flow during block transfers without aborting the entire operation.

features.name: Pause by Read Wait Signal
features.description:
## F_RW_READ_WAIT - Pause by Read Wait Signal

**Purpose:** This feature enables the host controller to pause an SDIO multi-block read operation by asserting the Read Wait signal on the DAT[2] line, allowing the host to temporarily halt data transfer when it cannot accept more data.

**Behavior:** When the host needs to pause during a read operation (e.g., buffer full or processing delay), it asserts the Read Wait signal, causing the SDIO card to stop sending data at the next block boundary. The card holds the data line in a wait state until the host de-asserts Read Wait, at which point the transfer resumes. This mechanism is essential for flow control in SDIO operations where the host may not be able to continuously receive data at the card's transmission rate.

features.name: Power Control
features.description:
# Power Control (F_POWER)

**Purpose:** Power Control manages the voltage supply to SD/SDIO cards, enabling the host controller to power on, power off, and select appropriate voltage levels (typically 3.3V or 1.8V) for connected cards.

**Behavior:** This feature controls the SD Bus Power register settings, allowing the host to enable/disable power delivery to the card slot and select the operating voltage based on card capabilities reported during initialization (via CMD5/R4 for SDIO). Proper power sequencing is critical for card initialization, voltage switching during UHS-I mode transitions, and implementing card removal/insertion handling with appropriate power cycling.

features.name: Master Power Control
features.description:
## Master Power Control (F_MASTER_POWER)

Master Power Control provides the top-level power management capability for the SD Host Controller, serving as the primary mechanism to enable or disable power delivery to connected SD/SDIO cards. This feature controls the main power rail switching, typically through the SD Bus Power bit in the Power Control Register, which must be properly sequenced during card initialization and removal.

As a P0 priority feature and parent to other power-related functions, it establishes the fundamental power state that all other power management features (voltage selection, power ramping, etc.) depend upon for proper operation.

features.name: Power Selection
features.description:
## F_POWER_SELECT (Power Selection)

**Purpose:** This feature enables the host controller to select and configure the appropriate voltage level for the SD/SDIO card interface, typically choosing between 3.3V and 1.8V signaling modes based on card capabilities and negotiation results.

**Behavior:** Power Selection works in conjunction with the parent power management feature (F_POWER) to dynamically switch voltage rails during card initialization and UHS-I mode transitions. The controller writes to power control registers to select the desired voltage, ensuring proper signal integrity and compliance with the card's supported voltage range as determined during the CMD5 (IO_SEND_OP_COND) exchange and subsequent voltage switching sequences.

features.name: Power State Control
features.description:
# Power State Control (F_POWER_STATE)

**Purpose:** Power State Control manages the transitions between different power states of the SD Host Controller and connected cards, including active, idle, sleep, and power-off states. This feature implements the state machine logic that coordinates voltage rail sequencing, clock gating, and signal line management during power state transitions.

**Behavior:** The controller monitors bus activity and host commands to determine appropriate power states, automatically transitioning cards to lower power modes during inactivity periods while ensuring proper wake-up sequences when activity resumes. It coordinates with the parent power management feature (F_POWER) to execute safe transitions that maintain card data integrity and comply with SDIO timing requirements for power state changes, including handling the specific wake-up signaling required for cards in sleep mode.

features.name: High-Speed Mode
features.description:
# High-Speed Mode (F_HIGH_SPEED)

High-Speed Mode enables the SDIO card and host controller to operate at increased clock frequencies up to 50 MHz, doubling the maximum data transfer rate compared to the default 25 MHz speed mode. This mode requires 4-bit SD data transfer capability (mandatory for High-Speed cards as specified in section 2.2.3) and involves negotiation between the host and card through the Card Capability registers to ensure both endpoints support the elevated timing requirements.

When enabled, High-Speed Mode allows theoretical maximum throughput of 200 Mb/s in 4-bit mode, making it essential for SDIO functions requiring higher bandwidth such as wireless networking or high-speed data acquisition applications.

features.name: Combo Card Speed Switching
features.description:
## Combo Card Speed Switching (F_HS_COMBO)

This feature enables High-Speed mode switching for SDIO Combo Cards, which contain both I/O functions and memory storage on a single card. When switching speeds on a combo card, the host controller must coordinate the speed transition for both the I/O and memory portions, typically requiring re-initialization sequences as described in section 3.4 to ensure both components operate synchronously at the new clock frequency.

The implementation must handle the special initialization considerations for combo cards, ensuring that speed mode changes are properly propagated to all card functions while maintaining data integrity across the shared bus interface.

features.name: CIS Tuple Formats
features.description:
## CIS Tuple Formats (F_CIS_FORMAT)

The CIS (Card Information Structure) Tuple Formats feature defines the standardized data structures used to encode card and function-specific information within the SDIO Card Information Structure. Each tuple consists of a type code, length byte, and variable-length data payload that describes capabilities such as manufacturer ID, function extensions, power requirements, and supported features.

This feature is essential for host controllers to properly parse and interpret the CIS data read from SDIO cards, enabling automatic configuration and capability discovery during card initialization and enumeration.

features.name: CISTPL_MANFID Tuple
features.description:
## CISTPL_MANFID Tuple (F_MANFID_TUPLE)

The CISTPL_MANFID tuple is a mandatory CIS (Card Information Structure) tuple that contains the manufacturer identification code and manufacturer-specific information code for an SDIO card or function. This tuple allows hosts to identify the card vendor and specific product variant, enabling vendor-specific driver loading and device recognition.

As a P1 priority feature within the CIS format hierarchy, this tuple must be present in the CIS and provides the SDIO Manufacturer Code (typically a JEDEC-assigned ID) and Manufacturer Information field that together uniquely identify the SDIO device for proper enumeration and driver binding.

features.name: CISTPL_FUNCID Tuple
features.description:
## CISTPL_FUNCID Tuple (F_FUNCID_TUPLE)

The CISTPL_FUNCID tuple is a mandatory Card Information Structure (CIS) tuple that identifies the function type/class of an SDIO function, using a standardized function identification code (such as UART, Bluetooth, WLAN, GPS, camera, etc.). This tuple enables the host system to determine what type of device driver or software stack is needed to communicate with the SDIO function.

As a P1 priority component of the CIS format hierarchy, this tuple must be present in each function's CIS area and provides the primary mechanism for automatic device classification and driver binding during SDIO card enumeration.

features.name: CISTPL_FUNCE Tuple
features.description:
## CISTPL_FUNCE Tuple (F_FUNCE_TUPLE)

The CISTPL_FUNCE (Function Extension) tuple is a CIS tuple type (code 0x22) that provides function-specific extended information for SDIO functions. This tuple contains detailed operational parameters such as maximum block size, supported transfer rates, power requirements, and timing specifications that are unique to each function within an SDIO card.

The FUNCE tuple format differs between Function 0 (common) and individual I/O functions (1-7), with Function 0's FUNCE containing card-wide capabilities while each function's FUNCE describes that specific function's operational characteristics and requirements for proper driver configuration.

features.name: Embedded SDIO
features.description:
## Embedded SDIO (F_EMBEDDED)

Embedded SDIO refers to SDIO devices that are permanently soldered onto a circuit board rather than being removable cards, commonly used for integrated WiFi, Bluetooth, or other connectivity modules in embedded systems. This configuration allows for optimizations such as eliminating card detection circuitry, using fixed voltage levels, and potentially simplified initialization sequences since the device characteristics are known at design time. The host controller may support specific features for embedded scenarios including back-end power control, interrupt signaling optimizations, and the ability to bypass certain enumeration steps defined in section 1.2.3 (Embedded SDIO Device Features).

features.name: Shared Bus Configuration
features.description:
Based on the specification context and the feature's placement in the embedded group, here is the description:

## Shared Bus Configuration (F_SHARED_BUS)

**Shared Bus Configuration** enables multiple embedded SDIO devices to share a common SD bus infrastructure within an embedded system. This feature allows the host controller to manage bus arbitration, device selection, and signal routing when multiple SDIO functions or devices are connected to the same physical bus lines, reducing pin count and board complexity in embedded designs.

The configuration typically involves interrupt sharing mechanisms, relative card address (RCA) management for multiple devices, and coordinated initialization sequences to ensure proper enumeration and operation of all devices on the shared bus without conflicts.

features.name: 8-Bit Bus Mode
features.description:
## 8-Bit Bus Mode (F_8BIT_BUS)

**Purpose:** Enables an 8-bit wide data bus interface for embedded SDIO devices, doubling the data transfer bandwidth compared to the standard 4-bit SD bus mode by utilizing all 8 data lines (DAT[7:0]).

**Behavior:** This feature is exclusive to embedded SDIO configurations where the host controller and SDIO device are integrated on the same board, allowing for the additional data lines that aren't available on standard SD card connectors. When enabled, the host controller configures its data path to transmit and receive data across 8 parallel data lines simultaneously, effectively achieving twice the throughput of 4-bit mode at the same clock frequency.
